_doc: Medication and condition interactions listed in the NIH ODS health-professional fact sheets (Interactions with Medications, and the health-risk sections for conditions). Only interactions named there are included; the list is not exhaustive. "kind": supplement_changes_drug | drug_lowers_nutrient | drug_raises_nutrient | additive_risk | two_way. Medication names are matched case-insensitively against generic and brand names; unknown names are normalized with NIH RxNorm when the service can reach it.

vitamin_k_antagonists.name: Warfarin and similar vitamin K antagonists

sjw_named_drugs.name: Drugs NIH names as weakened by St. John's wort

interactions.summary: Vitamin K counteracts warfarin; NIH describes a serious and potentially dangerous interaction. People on warfarin need a consistent vitamin K intake, because sudden changes raise or lower its anticoagulant effect.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin K fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Bile acid sequestrants can reduce vitamin K absorption, especially with long-term use.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin K fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Orlistat reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, K and beta-carotene); with warfarin it may markedly raise prothrombin time.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin K fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Large doses of vitamin E may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants, especially with low vitamin K intake; the amount needed is unknown but probably above 400 IU (about 180-270 mg) a day.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin E fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Large doses of vitamin E may increase bleeding risk with antiplatelet medications; the amount needed is unknown but probably above 400 IU a day.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin E fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: High-dose fish oil may prolong clotting time and raise INR with warfarin and similar anticoagulants, although 3-6 g a day usually does not change anticoagulant status; omega-3 drug labels advise periodic INR checks.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Omega-3 Fatty Acids fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Oral retinoids (acitretin, bexarotene, isotretinoin) taken with vitamin A supplements increase the risk of vitamin A toxicity.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin A fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Calcium supplements can sharply reduce dolutegravir levels.
interactions.timing: Take dolutegravir 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Calcium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Calcium carbonate can interfere with levothyroxine absorption.
interactions.timing: Avoid taking levothyroxine within 4 hours of calcium carbonate.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Calcium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Long-term lithium can cause high blood calcium; calcium supplements could add to that risk.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Calcium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Calcium reduces absorption of quinolone antibiotics.
interactions.timing: Take the antibiotic 2 hours before or 2 hours after calcium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Calcium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Iron may reduce levodopa absorption.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iron fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Iron taken at the same time can reduce levothyroxine efficacy.
interactions.timing: Separate levothyroxine and iron by at least 4 hours.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iron fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Proton pump inhibitors reduce iron absorption; iron-deficient patients on them may respond less well to iron supplements.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iron fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Magnesium-rich supplements may reduce absorption of oral bisphosphonates.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Magnesium binds tetracycline antibiotics and reduces their absorption.
interactions.timing: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after magnesium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Magnesium binds quinolone antibiotics and reduces their absorption.
interactions.timing: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after magnesium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Long-term loop diuretics increase magnesium loss in urine and may deplete it.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Long-term thiazide diuretics increase magnesium loss in urine and may deplete it.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Potassium-sparing diuretics reduce magnesium excretion.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Proton pump inhibitors taken for more than about a year can cause low blood magnesium, which supplements do not always correct; FDA advises checking magnesium levels.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Zinc and quinolone antibiotics reduce each other's absorption.
interactions.timing: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after zinc.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Zinc fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Zinc and tetracycline antibiotics reduce each other's absorption.
interactions.timing: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after zinc.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Zinc fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Zinc can reduce penicillamine absorption and action.
interactions.timing: Take zinc and penicillamine at least 1 hour apart.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Zinc fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Thiazide diuretics increase zinc loss in urine and lower blood zinc.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Zinc fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Orlistat reduces vitamin D absorption from food and supplements.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin D fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: High vitamin D intakes, especially from supplements, might reduce the potency of atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin; statins may also lower vitamin D synthesis.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin D fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Corticosteroids such as prednisone can reduce calcium absorption and impair vitamin D metabolism.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin D fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Thiazide diuretics reduce calcium loss in urine; with vitamin D supplements this might lead to high blood calcium, especially in older adults or people with reduced kidney function.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin D fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Folate supplements could interfere with methotrexate's anticancer effect (consult the oncologist); with low-dose methotrexate for arthritis or psoriasis, folate may reduce side effects.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Folate fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Antiepileptics such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and valproate can lower folate, and folate supplements may lower blood levels of these drugs.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Folate fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Sulfasalazine inhibits folate absorption and can cause folate deficiency.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Folate fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Proton pump inhibitors can reduce vitamin B12 absorption from food and lead to deficiency.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B12 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: H2 blockers can reduce vitamin B12 absorption from food and lead to deficiency.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B12 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Metformin might reduce vitamin B12 absorption and significantly lower blood B12.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B12 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Cycloserine increases vitamin B6 loss; supplements can help prevent its seizures and neurotoxicity.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B6 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Valproate, carbamazepine and phenytoin increase vitamin B6 breakdown; pyridoxine at 200 mg a day may lower blood levels of phenytoin and phenobarbital.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B6 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: People taking theophylline often have low vitamin B6, which could contribute to its side effects.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin B6 fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Isoniazid and pyrazinamide interfere with niacin production and can cause pellagra; more niacin can prevent it.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Niacin fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Large doses of nicotinic acid can raise blood glucose; glucose should be monitored and medication doses might need adjusting.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Niacin fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: ACE inhibitors reduce potassium excretion and can lead to high blood potassium; monitoring is recommended, especially with reduced kidney function.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Angiotensin receptor blockers reduce potassium excretion and can lead to high blood potassium; monitoring is recommended.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Potassium-sparing diuretics can cause high blood potassium; monitoring is recommended.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Loop diuretics increase potassium loss and can cause low blood potassium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Thiazide diuretics increase potassium loss and can cause low blood potassium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Cisplatin can lower selenium levels; the evidence that selenium reduces cisplatin toxicity is insufficient.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Selenium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: High-dose iodine with antithyroid medication may have an additive effect and cause hypothyroidism.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iodine fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Potassium iodide with ACE inhibitors may increase the risk of high blood potassium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iodine fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Potassium iodide with potassium-sparing diuretics may increase the risk of high blood potassium.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iodine fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Chromium may increase insulin sensitivity, raising the risk of low blood sugar with insulin.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Chromium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Chromium may lower blood glucose and add to diabetes medications, raising the risk of low blood sugar.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Chromium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Chromium picolinate taken at the same time reduced levothyroxine absorption in a small study.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Chromium fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Furosemide is linked to lower thiamin levels through urinary loss.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Thiamin fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Fluorouracil may increase thiamin breakdown; cases of beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy have been reported.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Thiamin fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

interactions.summary: Long-term anticonvulsants are linked to lower biotin levels.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Biotin fact sheet, Interactions with Medications

smoker.name: Current or former smoker, or asbestos exposure

checks.summary: Beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in smokers: 20 mg a day in the ATBC trial (lung cancer up 18%) and 30 mg a day with retinyl palmitate in CARET (up 28%). NIH considers large supplemental doses harmful for current or former smokers and people exposed to asbestos.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin A and Carotenoids fact sheet

kidney_disease.name: Chronic kidney disease or reduced kidney function

checks.summary: With reduced kidney function, potassium is cleared poorly; NIH notes even intakes below the AI can cause high blood potassium. Check potassium-containing supplements and salt substitutes with a clinician.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Potassium fact sheet

checks.summary: Impaired kidney function raises the risk of magnesium toxicity from supplements and magnesium-containing laxatives and antacids, because the kidneys cannot remove the excess.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet

checks.summary: People with chronic kidney disease are prone to high blood phosphate and are usually advised to limit phosphorus; check phosphorus-containing supplements with a clinician.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Phosphorus fact sheet

checks.summary: People with hereditary hemochromatosis absorb too much iron; iron supplements add to iron overload.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Iron fact sheet

checks.summary: In hereditary hemochromatosis, chronic high-dose vitamin C could worsen iron overload and cause tissue damage, because it increases iron absorption.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin C fact sheet

lab_test_soon.name: Blood test coming up (thyroid, troponin, hormone or vitamin D tests)

checks.summary: High-dose biotin can make some laboratory tests (thyroid hormones, troponin, vitamin D and others) read falsely high or low; a single 10 mg dose interfered with thyroid tests drawn within 24 hours, and the FDA reported a death after a falsely low troponin result. Tell the clinician and lab about biotin.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Biotin fact sheet

checks.summary: Oncologists generally advise checking antioxidant supplements such as vitamin C during chemotherapy and radiation, because they might reduce treatment effectiveness; the evidence is mixed.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin C fact sheet

checks.summary: Oncologists generally advise against antioxidant supplements such as vitamin E during chemotherapy and radiation, because they might reduce treatment effectiveness; a systematic review has questioned this.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin E fact sheet
